newsitem.title: USA: Galileo Int'l IPO seen well received.
newsitem.headline: Galileo Int'l IPO seen well received.

text.p: Electronic reservations company Galileo International Inc's stable business and solid growth should garner respectable, if unspectacular, gains for its $688 million initial public offering.

The offering of 31.998 million shares is expected to price between $20 and $23 a share. As of 1820 EST, the deal had not been priced, but lead underwriter Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said it was still expected to price later on Thursday for trading on Friday.
The opening premium "could be three (dollars) plus," said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket newsletter.
Galileo is owned by 11 North American and European airlines, and provides global distribution services for the travel industry.

Its computerized reservation system allows travel agencies to access schedule and fare information, make reservations and issue tickets for 525 airlines. The system also provides access to 48 car rental companies and over 200 major hotel chains.
"It's a stable business," said Ryan Jacob, director of research at IPO Value Monitor. "A lot of their investors are also their customers."
Shareholders in the global reservation company include UAL Corp's United Airlines, US Airways Group, British Airways Plc, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV and Swissair.

Mark Basham, investment officer at Standard & Poor's, said he was recommending Galileo, but viewed its closest competitor, Sabre Group Holdings Inc, with a slightly more favorable eye because of the outsourcing business Sabre carried out for companies both in and out of the travel industry. This, he said, made Sabre less vulnerable to softness in the economy that could dampen travel demand.

But analysts were, on the whole, upbeat about Galileo's prospects. "They've got good profit margins... they have good presence both internationally and domestically.. there's good growth opportunities abroad, with most countries outside of the U.S. not having the level of automation in the travel industry that the U.S does," said Ken Fleming, analyst at Renaissance Capital Corp.
According to its filing, more than half of Galileo's 1996 revenues were derived from bookings outside of the U.S.

Fleming said that the one thing that could hold the deal back was the fact that Sabre has had a mediocre stock performance since its October 1996 IPO. The stock ran up to 33-3/8 from the IPO price of $27 a share, but then slipped down to a low of 23-1/4 before recovering somewhat. It closed at 29-7/8 on Thursday.

However, he said, Galileo's arrival on the scene could draw more attention to the business and benefit both companies. "Sabre was very unique when it came out, and now that Galileo is coming out it could bring more attention to the area and help both Sabre and Galileo."

According to Galileo's filing, it intends to use the proceeds of the offering to fund acquisitions of certain national distribution companies (NDCs). It said it expects to buy Apollo Travel Services Partnership for $700 million, Traviswiss AG for $8 million and, subject to Dutch regulatory approval, Galileo Nederland BV for a price of $2 million.
These distribution companies market Galileo's products in the United States, Mexico, certain Carribean islands, Switzerland and The Netherlands.
Apollo is majority owned by UAL Corp's United Airlines, which also holds a 38 percent stake in Galileo.

The company said that upon completion of the offering, airline stockholders will own about 68 percent of its outstanding common stock, or 65 percent if the underwriters' overallotment option is exercised. United Airlines and KLM will be the largest shareholders.
Galileo had revenues of $1.088 billion in 1996, up from $966.4 million in 1995.
